clinicalPearls: CJD is a rapidly progressive disorder associated with dementia, focal cortical signs, rigidity, and myoclonus, causing death less than 1 year after first symptoms appear (p.3525-3526).

CJD is the classic cause of a rapidly progressive dementia (RPD: progression from symptom onset to dementia within a year or less), especially when associated with myoclonus, though more often RPD is due to AD, another neurodegenerative disorder, or autoimmune encephalitis (p.237).
On examination, CJD is suggested by diffuse rigidity, an akinetic-mute state, and prominent, often startle-sensitive myoclonus (p.239).

MRI diffusion-weighted imaging reveals restricted diffusion within the cortical ribbon and/or basal ganglia in most patients; basal ganglia or thalamus hyperintensity may also be seen on diffusion/FLAIR MRI (p.240, p.3526).
EEG is not routinely used but can suggest CJD by showing repetitive bursts of diffuse high-amplitude sharp waves (periodic complexes) (p.241).

Prion diseases such as CJD are rare (prevalence ~1 per million); the rapidity of progression distinguishes CJD from AD, though AD can occasionally present as a rapidly progressive dementia (p.3525-3526).
Prion disease is one cause of subacute progressive ataxia, especially when an infectious etiology such as transmission from contaminated human growth hormone is responsible (p.3590).
harrison.pathophysiology: Prion diseases are caused by prions, host-encoded proteins (the prion protein) that adopt an alternative, abnormal conformation (misfolded PrPSc) which undergoes self-propagation. PrPSc imposes its conformation on the normal precursor protein, which in turn becomes self-templating, producing faithful copies; the misfolded protein is enriched for beta-sheet and assembles into amyloid fibrils. The amyloid plaques in kuru and CJD are filled with PrPSc prions assembled into fibrils. CJD is one of the major degenerative dementias characterized by abnormal aggregation of a specific protein (misfolded prion protein, PrPSc). Familial CJD is genetically linked to mutations in the PrP gene (p.237, p.3400-3401).
additionalDifferentials: Alzheimer's disease (can occasionally present as rapidly progressive dementia)
Corticobasal degeneration (CBD) - rapid degenerative dementia with prominent movement abnormalities, more likely mistaken for CJD
Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) - rapid degenerative dementia with prominent movement abnormalities, more likely mistaken for CJD
infectionMimics: Other CNS infections causing rapidly progressive dementia
nonInfectiousMimics: Prolonged focal or generalized seizures (can rarely produce a similar imaging appearance)
additionalInvestigations: MRI diffusion-weighted imaging - restricted diffusion in cortical ribbon and/or basal ganglia (cortical ribboning); basal ganglia or thalamus hyperintensity on diffusion/FLAIR
EEG - periodic complexes (repetitive bursts of diffuse high-amplitude sharp waves)
Lumbar puncture/CSF - to exclude CNS infection or inflammation among rapidly progressive dementia mimics
MRI/neuroimaging to exclude treatable structural causes (neoplasm, subdural hematoma, NPH)
redFlags: Rapidly progressive dementia (onset to dementia within a year or less)
Cortical ribboning / basal ganglia or thalamic hyperintensity on diffusion/FLAIR MRI
harrison.prognosis: Uniformly fatal. CJD causes death less than 1 year after the first symptoms appear (p.3525-3526).
pitfalls: Must exclude treatable causes of rapidly progressive dementia (e.g., autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis, Hashimoto's encephalopathy, CNS vasculitis, CNS infection, lymphoma) before attributing a rapidly progressive dementia to CJD.
More rapid degenerative dementias with prominent movement abnormalities (CBD, DLB) are more likely to be mistaken for CJD.
Rarely, prolonged focal or generalized seizures can produce an MRI appearance similar to CJD.
harrison.severityClassification: Etiologic classification of prion diseases (all caused by PrPSc): sporadic (e.g., classic CJD), familial/genetic (linked to PrP gene mutations - includes familial CJD, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker disease [GSS], and fatal insomnia), iatrogenic (transmission e.g. from contaminated human growth hormone), and acquired/transmissible forms (kuru). PrPSc prions also cause animal spongiform encephalopathies including scrapie, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), and chronic wasting disease (p.3400-3401, p.3590).
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; care is supportive and directed at comfort throughout the rapidly progressive, uniformly fatal course
Symptomatic control of myoclonus with antimyoclonic agents such as clonazepam, levetiracetam or valproate
Manage agitation, spasticity and rigidity, and treat distressing psychiatric and behavioural symptoms
Nursing care for progressive immobility and dysphagia, with attention to aspiration risk, skin integrity and nutrition/feeding decisions
Early palliative care involvement and advance care planning given the rapid decline and poor prognosis

Infection-control and public-health measures: statutory notification, single-use or specialised instrument decontamination for neurosurgical and ophthalmic procedures, and referral to the national prion surveillance unit
Genetic counselling and family testing for familial (PrP gene) disease
